Yes. 

The manipulation of time in the story is very well-balanced and serves the quiet, atmospheric mood of the narrative. The entire "story time" consists of a single, brief ferry crossing across a river, which broadly aligns with the "real world time" it takes to read the piece. 

Within that real-time framework, the author skillfully uses **compression** to weave in decades of backstory—such as Ilse's twenty-three years of experience on the ferry, the changing of the seasons on the river, and the histories of the local passengers—into brief, observational sentences. This grounds the setting without disrupting the flow of the crossing. Conversely, at the end of the story, the author uses **stretching** when Ilse's phone rings. The brief seconds of the phone vibrating are drawn out through sensory details (the vibration traveling through her glove and up her arm) and observations of the other passengers, which effectively builds quiet tension and highlights the emotional weight of the unanswered call.
